summary: (a Govt. of India Enterprise) NHPC Office Complex, Sector-33, Faridabad (Haryana)- 121003. ** Petitioner** The instant Review Petition has been filed by the Review Petitioner, NHPC Limited (NHPC), seeking a review of the Commission’s order dated 19.6.2025 in Petition No. 87/AT/2025 (the ‘impugned order’), whereby the Commission approved the tariff for the supply of the 1200 MW power from Inter-State Transmission System (“ **ISTS** ”) connected Firm and Dispatchable Power (“ **FDRE** ”) from Renewable Energy Power Generators (“ **RE-PG** ”) with Energy Storage Systems (“ **ESS** ”) selected through competitive bidding process. The prayers urged in the present Review Petition are as under: _(c) Issue amendment to Para 31 of order dated 19.06.2025 in petition No. 87/AT/2025._ _(d) Pass such other and further order / orders as are deemed fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case._ ” b) The Commission in the impugned order dated 19.6.2025 has acknowledged the existence of ‘Greenshoe Option’. 5. The matter was heard on 27.11.2025. After hearing the parties, the matter was reserved for order. 6. The instant Review Petition has been filed under Section 94(1) of the Act read with Section 114 and Order 47 Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as ‘CPC’) and Regulation 52 (2) (B) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023 (hereinafter referred to as “CBR, 2023”) seeking review of the order dated 19.6.2025 passed by the Commission in Petition No. 87/AT/2025. Regulation 52(2) of the CBR, 2023 provides that an aggrieved party can seek review of a direction, decision or order of the Commission, which is akin to the grounds provided in Order 47 Rule 1 of the CPC. The Review Petitioner has submitted that at paragraphs 31 & 32 of the impugned Order, the Commission only adopted the tariff for allocated capacity to the respective bidders but not the capacity allocated under the Greenshoe Option to such bidders despite having acknowledged the same. _“(1) The Commission shall exercise jurisdiction to review its own orders, decisions, and directions in accordance with Clause (f) of sub-section (1) of Section 94 of the Act read with Section 114 and Order 47 of the Civil Procedure Code._ _(2) Any person aggrieved by a direction, decision, or order of the Commission, from which no appeal has been preferred, may file a review petition on the 34 following grounds within forty days of the making of such decision, direction, or order:_ _(a) Upon the discovery of new and important matter or evidence that, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the direction, decision, or order was passed or;_ 9. It is noted that the Review Petitioner had filed Petition No. 87/AT/2025 along “(a) _Admit the present Petition. (b) Adopt the_ _**Tariff discovered in the Competitive Bidding Process for individual Power Projects as listed in Table-1 at paragraph 9** above on terms and conditions contained in the PPA to be signed with RE-Power Generators being Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and a Trading Margin of Rs. 0.07 / kWh in addition to above Tariff is to be recovered from buying Utilities /Distribution Licensee/DISCOM(s) in terms of the PSA to be signed between NHPC & Utilities/ Distribution Licensee._ _(c ) Pass such other and further order / orders as are deemed fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case._ ” 12. Therefore, the Review Petitioner has failed to incorporate any specific prayer seeking the relief now claimed in the Review Petition. It is a cornerstone of procedural jurisprudence that no court or tribunal possesses the inherent power to grant a relief not expressly pleaded or prayed for, as this would deny counter-parties a fair opportunity to address the claim and imperil the adversarial process. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of _Bharat Amratlal Kothari v. Dosukhan Samadkhan Sindhi [(AIR 2010 SC 475)]_ has held that a tribunal cannot grant relief not prayed for, disregarding established norms governing the grant of relief. 13. It is apposite to note that the power of the Commission to review its order is concededly restricted and can be exercised only in certain specific circumstances and is limited to errors that are self-evident, without requiring elaborate arguments or interpretation. The Review Petitioner has invoked the provisions of Section 94(1)(f) of the Act and Regulation 52 of the CBR, 2023, on the ground of an ‘error apparent on the face of the record’ in the impugned order for failing to adopt the tariff pertaining to the ‘Greenshoe option’ quantum. However, as seen above, the order passed by the Commission was confined to the prayers specifically sought by NHPC during the hearing of Petition No. 87/AT/2025. No such patent error has been demonstrated by the Review Petitioner. 14. For the reasons aforementioned, we find no merit in the submissions advanced by the Review Petitioner so as to warrant the entertainment of the present Review Petition. The Review Petition does not disclose any error apparent on the face of the record that merits exercise of review jurisdiction under Section 94(1)(f) of the Act read with Regulation 52 of the CBR, 2023. Accordingly, the Review Petition is rejected. However, considering the important nature of the matter which pertains to green power, the Petitioner is granted liberty to file a fresh Petition specifically seeking adoption of the ‘Greenshoe Option’ quantum, and the same shall be considered in accordance with law.
